topic: std::multiset::insert Return Value and Duplicate Handling
explanation:
Unlike `std::set`, which returns a `std::pair<iterator, bool>` to indicate whether the insertion occurred and the position, `std::multiset` permits duplicate keys. Consequently, the `insert(const value_type& val)` member function always succeeds (unless memory allocation fails) and returns a single `iterator` pointing directly to the newly inserted element.

Purpose: This simple return signature reflects the fact that insertion is guaranteed, simplifying code compared to checking the boolean status required by `std::set`.

Technical Details: Insertion complexity is logarithmic in the size of the container, O(log N). If the element is inserted using the hint version `insert(iterator hint, const value_type& val)`, and the hint is correct, complexity can be amortized constant time O(1). The returned iterator points to a valid, newly constructed element within the container.

Pitfalls: The returned iterator must not be dereferenced if the container operation threw an exception (e.g., bad_alloc). Relying on the position of the inserted element (as shown in the text using `distance`) is generally discouraged, as the relative position of duplicates is not strictly defined by the standard, though it is usually stable based on insertion order for equal keys.
practical_example: When implementing a scheduling queue where tasks with identical priorities (the key) must all be tracked, `std::multiset` is used. The returned iterator allows immediate access to the newly added task object for further modification or logging, without needing to search for it again.
book: The C++ Standard Library: A Tutorial and Reference by Nicolai M. Josuttis
